name: Obestatin

lead: Obestatin is a peptide made from the same gene as the hunger hormone ghrelin. A 2005 paper in Science reported that it reduced appetite in rodents, which led fat-loss readers to see it as a possible diet aid for lower intake and fat loss.
Other labs could not confirm the appetite effect, and its proposed receptor GPR39 was later found to respond to zinc instead. No studies test it for weight or appearance in people.

paras: There is no product; it is discussed as a hormone of the appetite system rather than something people use.
No approved product exists and the sources reviewed give no human safety data for administering it.

angle.text: Obestatin is a ghrelin-gene peptide first reported to curb appetite, so fat-loss readers see it as a possible diet aid for lower intake and fat loss. Later studies could not reproduce the appetite effect, and its receptor is disputed.

lead: Obestatin is a 23-residue peptide encoded by the same gene as ghrelin. It was reported in Science in 2005 as opposing ghrelin's effects on food intake, and it was found through computer analysis of genome sequences.[1][2]

Its reported appetite-suppressing effect and its receptor have both been disputed. Later studies found that GPR39, first proposed as its receptor, responds to zinc ions but not obestatin, and some groups could not reproduce its effects on food intake.[3][4][5]
Obestatin is an endogenous peptide. The sources reviewed describe no approved use and no trial of it as a treatment.

paras: The 2005 Science paper described obestatin as derived from preproghrelin and reported that it reduced food intake and body weight gain in rodents, opposing ghrelin.[1][2]

Holst and colleagues reported that GPR39 signalling is stimulated by zinc but not by obestatin, and another group reported the same.[3][4] A 2007 rodent study examined obestatin's effects on energy balance and growth hormone secretion.[5] Wikipedia notes that other researchers reported no effect on food intake and that natural production of obestatin by a specific enzyme has not been shown.[2] Reviews have discussed how ghrelin gene products differ in their actions on intake and gut motility.[6]
Circulating obestatin has been measured in obesity, diabetes and other conditions, and a 2011 meta-analysis examined ghrelin and obestatin levels in relation to obesity.[2]

No studies found of obestatin as a treatment for appearance or body weight. Registered human studies with ghrelin (not obestatin) examine appetite in cancer and other settings, and one observational study measured ghrelin and obestatin in children with chronic kidney disease.[7][8]
